distinguishing_features: Detects oil accumulation (mass logging) in evaporator tubes via induced mass-per-length increase, rather than lubricant film-thickness/stiffness degradation in a bearing.
Uses a downward shift in the tube's structural natural frequency (mass loading) as the indicator, instead of a stiffness-driven frequency drop in a rotor-bearing system.
Senses the resonance through existing pressure-transducer noise/FFT rather than an existing vibration sensor's spectral centroid.
Treats oil as an added-mass contaminant in a heat-exchanger flow path, not as a lubricant whose film thickness is degrading.
parsed.objective_technical_problem: Detect early accumulation of oil (mass logging) inside evaporator tubes, before capacity loss, using only existing pressure sensors and no added hardware.
parsed.viable_reason: As written the stated magnitude is self-defeating: a 1 mm-wall, 12 mm-ID steel tube has steel mass per length far exceeding a 10% oil fill, so the claimed 15% mu increase and 7% frequency drop are physically implausible, and pressure-noise FFT excitation of a liquid-filled tube resonance is unvalidated.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: Although the added-mass-to-frequency-shift idea parallels prior-art resonance inference, applying it to oil logging via pressure-sensor FFT for a heat-exchanger evaporator is not a routine parameter change from bearing/vibration art.
